newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Top HK judge resigns to seek post-1997 leadership.
newsitem.headline: Top HK judge resigns to seek post-1997 leadership.

text.p: Hong Kong's top judge quit on Friday to contest the territory's first non-colonial leadership while Beijing drew cautious applause for signalling it would keep the process of picking the new chief transparent.

Chief Justice Sir Ti Liang Yang resigned after he announced earlier this week he would run for the job as Hong Kong's chief executive when Britain hands back the territory to China on midnight June 30, 1997.
Yang, 67, had been under pressure to resign due to a potential conflict of interest which legal experts and politicians said raised a question mark over his role in the British-style judiciary.

"In a letter to the governor, Sir Ti Liang stated that following his decision to accept nomination to the post (of) chief executive of the Special Administrative Region of Hong Kong, constitutional propriety required him to resign from the post of Chief Justice," a government statement said.
Newly proposed rules on how that leader would be selected also were welcomed in the nervous British colony.

Hong Kong government radio reported that a set of rules worked out by a panel in Beijing on Thursday would make it possible for the public to see who was backing whom in the process of choosing the chief executive.

"The procedures for selection of the chief executive proposed in Beijing... provide a welcome recognition of the importance of transparency in picking the person who will guide Hong Kong's future," the South China Morning Post said.

The chief executive who will take over from Governor Chris Patten on July 1, 1997, will be chosen by a 400-member Selection Committee, itself to be named soon by Beijing's Preparatory Committee overseeing the handover -- that much was known.
But many fear the committee would just rubber-stamp a candidate pre-approved by Beijing, without much debate on who the candidate was or what he or she stood for.

On Thursday, a panel of the Preparatory Committee proposed each candidate should be nominated by at least 50 members of the Selection Committee, and that the names of the nominators should be published, government radio reported.

That allows for scrutiny by the Hong Kong public and press of exactly who is backing each candidate. The number on nominators was also cut from 100, raising the number of possible candidates to eight, and allowing more committee members to avoid having to pledge their support too early in the process.
The candidates will have to present themselves to the committee in front of the media, reports from Beijing said.
"The accounts they provide of their intentions -- and perhaps a full electoral platform -- will thus be passed on to the public through the press, radio and television," the Post said.
The 400 members of the committee would then vote by secret ballot, with support of at least half required for election.

The race already has some competition. In addition to Yang, prominent lawyer Lo Tak-shing has also declared his candidacy, and shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa, widely tipped to be Beijing's favourite, is also expected to throw his name in soon.
Hong Kong's favourite is Patten's deputy, Anson Chan, but her close association with the British administration is widely regarded as ruling her out in Beijing's eyes.
But not everyone was convinced by Beijing's softer tone.
"I think there may be a bit of an effort to make it look less secretive, it's like the general Chinese charm offensive of the last couple of weeks," said China watcher Jonathan Mirsky.
